{"id": "69:18/q22", "question": "What is the 'khāfiyah' that cannot remain hidden?", "turns_on": "Whether the concealed item is an act, person, inner state, nakedness, or a person's moral and religious standing.", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q22/p1", "position": "It is a hidden deed or act.", "reasons": "Ibn Shajara specifies deeds people used to conceal; Ibn ʿAbbās includes hidden acts and traits. Al-Kalbī says no deed is hidden; Ibn ʿĀshūr says a feminine implicit act can be understood. Asad stresses even the most hidden deed. Other sources also allow a person as an alternative."}, {"id": "69:18/q22/p2", "position": "It is a hidden person or soul: no one evades judgment.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies neither righteous nor wicked person is concealed. Al-Iṣlāḥī says nothing remains in the destroyed heavens and earth to hide a person. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds that no confusion remains between believer and unbeliever or virtuous and wicked. Study Quran reports Q's translation 'None among you shall be hidden.'"}, {"id": "69:18/q22/p3", "position": "It is any inner secret, thought, belief, state, or concealed thing.", "reasons": "Jishumī derives khāfiyah from concealment, the opposite of public disclosure. Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives an inner thought or conviction; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Nasafī mention formerly hidden states. Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes beliefs and deeds and cites 86:9 and 40:16. Study Quran's R says disclosure brings believers joy and disbelievers grief. Al-Ṭabrisī also permits the verbal noun 'anything hidden.'"}, {"id": "69:18/q22/p4", "position": "It may mean exposed nakedness: no private parts remain covered.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī quotes the Prophet that people are gathered barefoot and naked; al-Qurṭubī gives the same report as the basis for this interpretation."}, {"id": "69:18/q22/p5", "position": "It entails the visible distinction of believers from unbelievers and the righteous from the wicked.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr gives the distinction; Ibn ʿĀshūr says no confusion between the groups remains."}]}

{"id": "69:18/q24", "question": "What does 'at its edges' in the adjacent verse mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q24/p1", "position": "Arjāʾihā means its sides or regions.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says singular rajā has a short alif written against the pattern of ramā, supported by rajawān and cited poetry."}]}
{"id": "71:17/q01", "question": "What does أَنۢبَتَكُم mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the plant verb is read as an expression for creation or for the process of growth.", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q01/p1", "position": "It means God created or originated humans, expressed as causing growth.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls nabāt creation; al-Damghani gives 'create' as a sense of anbata. Ibn ʿAshur compares the likeness to human formation from earth's elements, 3:37, and the idiom 'God planted you for good.' Al-Alusi says growth makes origination from earth visible."}, {"id": "71:17/q01/p2", "position": "It means to cause growth or bring forth progressively.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi describes a plant emerging from earth stage by stage. Elmalılı explains anbata as making grow or bringing forth; growth in vegetation occurs through nourishment and reproduction. Asad describes gradual human growth."}]}
{"id": "71:17/q02", "question": "Is the comparison of human creation to plant growth figurative or literal?", "turns_on": "Whether shared earthly material and growth make the plant comparison literal or a metaphor for origination.", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q02/p1", "position": "It is a metaphor for humans being originated from earth.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin call the growth language metaphorical, connecting Adam's earthly origin to his descendants. Al-Baydawi says the image conveys coming into being and formation especially well. Al-Alusi calls it an explicit transferred verbal metaphor, treating resurrection deniers as if they denied origination too. Ibn ʿAshur stresses the close likeness to plants through common earthly elements."}, {"id": "71:17/q02/p2", "position": "It speaks literally of bodies growing from specially combined earthly elements.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i says those elements nourish bodies, support growth and reproduction, and constitute the reality of plant growth. Asad also identifies organic and inorganic earthly substances in each developing body."}]}
{"id": "71:17/q03", "question": "In what sense did God grow humans from the earth?", "turns_on": "Whether the earthly origin is traced through Adam, each person's nourishment and elements, personal maturation, species development, or an inward account of the body.", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q03/p1", "position": "Adam was made from earth, and the address includes his descendants through him.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj says Adam was made from soil of the whole earth; Qurtubi points to discussions in al-Anʿam and al-Baqara. Khalid ibn Maʿdan says humanity was made from clay and links this to hearts softening in winter. Al-Kalbi, al-Wahidi and others explain descent from Adam. Al-Tabrisi cites 4:1; al-Razi, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿAshur and Study Quran cite 3:59, the dust origin of Adam, with Study Quran noting the Adam–Jesus likeness."}, {"id": "71:17/q03/p2", "position": "All people arise from earth through food, plants, nutrients, semen, or their bodily elements.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas traces the sperm drop to earth; al-Razi specifies nutrients to plants to food to semen. Al-Mawardi and al-Tabrisi refer to nourishment from earth's growth and substances; al-Biqaʿi says earth supplies food. Bursawi includes the chain of sperm, plants and food. Elmalılı reports this alongside Adam's origin. Kur'an Yolu notes direct or indirect nourishment. Tabataba'i and Asad stress earthly elements; Asad connects this to stages in 71:14. Ibn ʿAshur says human bodies are formed from earth's elements like plants."}, {"id": "71:17/q03/p3", "position": "The growth is each person's development from infancy or smallness to maturity and height.", "reasons": "Ibn Baḥr and al-Tabrisi describe movement from smallness to largeness or old age and from shortness to height. Ibn Jurayj, as reported by Qurtubi, describes humans growing on earth from childhood to adulthood and increasing in height."}, {"id": "71:17/q03/p4", "position": "It also refers to the human species evolving from primitive organisms through increasingly complex development.", "reasons": "Asad extends the successive stages to bodily, mental and spiritual development of the species."}, {"id": "71:17/q03/p5", "position": "In an inward reading, it is the growth of the body from its earthly basis.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani speaks of emergence from the 'earth of the body.' Bursawi reports people of spiritual knowledge who liken bodily nourishment and growth from earth to plants drawing on water and soil."}]}
{"id": "71:17/q04", "question": "What does مِّنَ mark in مِّنَ ٱلْأَرْضِ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q04/p1", "position": "It marks the earth as the remote origin of creation.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi explicitly calls min originative and the origin remote."}]}
{"id": "71:17/q05", "question": "What can نَبَاتًۭا mean as a noun?", "turns_on": "Whether nabāt is taken as an action noun or a noun for vegetation or the result.", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q05/p1", "position": "It is a verbal noun meaning sprouting or growing.", "reasons": "Elmalılı gives this sense alongside the collective noun. {"id": "71:17/q06", "question": "How is نَبَاتًۭا governed and parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether nabāt can be governed directly by anbata through shared meaning, requires an omitted growth verb or paired ellipsis, serves as a circumstance, or belongs to an implicit planting of vegetation.", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q06/p1", "position": "It is an accusative verbal noun attached to أَنۢبَتَكُم by shared meaning, standing for the regular إنباتًا.", "reasons": "Sibawayh licenses a nonmatching verbal noun when meanings coincide, comparing اجتوروا/تجاوروا, انكسر/كسر, al-Qatami's تتبعه اتباعا, Ruʾba's تطويت انطواء, and يدعه تركا. Al-Akhfash, al-Nahhas, al-Thaʿlabi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, al-Suyuti, Bursawi, Elmalılı and Ibn ʿAshur distinguish regular inbāt from nabāt. Al-Zajjaj and Abu Isḥāq say 'made you grow' licenses the sense and adds emphasis. Ibn Qutayba compares tabtīlan at 73:8, two poets' ittibāʿan and ʿiwādan, and shared meanings of different verbs. Abu Hayyan and al-Samin call deletion of added letters an ism maṣdar. Al-Zarkashi allows direct government when meanings match; Elmalılı says a verbal noun is the prior, stronger analysis, since people are not simply plants. Ibn Kathir calls this noun particularly apt; Islahi says the verbal nouns emphasize their verbs in different ways."}, {"id": "71:17/q06/p2", "position": "An omitted 'you grew' governs نَبَاتًۭا: God made you grow, so you grew.", "reasons": "Al-Khalil supplies fa-nabattum nabātan; al-Mubarrad gives the same parse, which Ibn Khuruf chose and Ibn Yaʿish accepted. Ibn al-Jawzi compares the growth in 3:37. Al-Zamakhshari alternatively treats anbata as containing the sense of nabattum; al-Samin identifies tha

{"id": "71:17/q07", "question": "Was the omitted-verb analysis rightly attributed to Sibawayh?", "turns_on": "The historical attribution of the parsing to Sibawayh.", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q07/p1", "position": "It was attributed to Sibawayh.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi reports this attribution while citing al-Mubarrad's omitted-verb analysis and the support of Ibn Khuruf and Ibn Yaʿish."}, {"id": "71:17/q07/p2", "position": "Ibn ʿAsfur disputes that attribution.", "reasons": "His dispute concerns the attribution, rather than necessarily the validity of the omitted-verb parse."}]}
{"id": "71:17/q08", "question": "Why use the growth wording and نَبَاتًۭا rather than a plain statement of creation?", "turns_on": "Whether the noteworthy force is visible proof, the emphatic and lighter noun, or compressed expression by entailment.", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q08/p1", "position": "It makes divine origination observable and the argument perceptible.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says God's act itself is unseen and would otherwise need revelation, whereas marvelous complete growth is seen. Ibn Kathir calls the noun especially apt."}, {"id": "71:17/q08/p2", "position": "The lighter noun or altered form gives emphasis and eloquence, and can suggest ease or elaborate, powerful creation.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and Abu Isḥāq find nabāt more emphatic than the regular inbāt. {"id": "71:17/q09", "question": "What parallel readings are mentioned while explaining the wording?", "turns_on": "These are different cited passages and readers, not rival readings of 71:17.", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q09/p1", "position": "A reading attributed to Ibn Masʿud has 'wa-anzala l-malāʾikata tanzīlā' at 25:25.", "reasons": "Sibawayh uses the shared meanings of anzala and nazzala to illustrate a nonmatching verbal noun."}, {"id": "71:17/q09/p2", "position": "Abu ʿAmr reads 'mimmā khaṭāyāhum' with yāʾ, while the other readers use 'khaṭīʾātihim' with tāʾ, lengthening and hamza.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi reports these readings in the surrounding discussion; he also says the variant in waladuhu was treated under Surat Maryam 19:77."}]}
{"id": "71:17/q10", "question": "How does this verse connect to the nearby signs and the resurrection?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection is the sequence of signs and resurrection or the continued syntax of the earlier rhetorical question.", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q10/p1", "position": "After heavenly signs, the passage turns to humans and the earth as a proof of creation and resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says the verse returns to proofs in human selves and stages of creation, relating 71:14 to earth, return, and emergence; he calls it the third proof of oneness. Islahi calls humans earth's noblest creatures and likens human death and return to vegetation dying and returning; renewed plants show God's power to raise people. Asad relates bodily stages to 71:14."}, {"id": "71:17/q10/p2", "position": "The verse continues a rhetorical question begun in verse 15.", "reasons": "Study Quran says verse 16 may begin 'and that He' and verses 17 and 19 continue the same question."}]}

{"id": "71:17/q12", "question": "What does this sign ask people to recognize about God?", "turns_on": "Which inference from earthly growth the commentator draws: sole worship, resurrection, or the one source of beings.", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q12/p1", "position": "God alone creates and provides, so He alone deserves worship.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi says the favors prove God's exclusive claim to worship, His knowledge of human interests and wise governance, and condemn disbelief. Ibn ʿAshur calls it an embedded promise of life after death. Islahi argues from renewed vegetation to God's ability to revive people at will."}, {"id": "71:17/q12/p3", "position": "The diversity of growing beings points to one ontological source in God.", "reasons": "Study Quran says all things emerge from God as one Source, whose substance is within them."}]}
{"id": "71:17/q13", "question": "How is this sign framed by the sūra's overall purpose?", "turns_on": "Whether the broader framing emphasizes Noah's preaching, the threat and resurrection, or the symbolic spiritual struggle.", "positions": [{"id": "71:17/q13/p1", "position": "Noah's preaching uses creation and provision as signs in his call to his people.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir says Noah invokes divine power, greatness and heavenly and earthly benefits. Asad calls the Meccan sūra entirely devoted to Noah's preaching to his erring people, comparing 11:25."}, {"id": "71:17/q13/p2", "position": "Noah's story demonstrates God's power to destroy rejecters, replace them, and raise the dead.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi says the people's destruction for rejecting Noah establishes the threat. {"id": "71:18/q01", "question": "What does ثم convey before the return to earth?", "turns_on": "Whether ثم orders events by time or orders the argument by importance.", "positions": [{"id": "71:18/q01/p1", "position": "It marks the long interval from creation to death and burial.", "reasons": "Alusi says that people live under obligations and earn recompense during this interval."}, {"id": "71:18/q01/p2", "position": "It marks a rise in importance to the warning of resurrection, with burial preparing for that main point.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the resurrection warning matters more than the prior proof from creation, so the ordering is by rank rather than elapsed time."}]}
{"id": "71:18/q02", "question": "What is God's returning people into the earth?", "turns_on": "Whether the return is physical burial or an inward attachment to the material world.", "positions": [{"id": "71:18/q02/p1", "position": "People die and are buried in the earth, their bodies returning to it.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Tabrisi specify corpses in graves; Ibn Atiyya calls burial customary human practice. {"id": "71:18/q05", "question": "What is the grammatical form of إخراجا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "71:18/q05/p1", "position": "It is the regular إفعال verbal noun of an أفعل verb, within the system of augmented verb forms.", "reasons": "Sibawayh gives يخرجكم إخراجا as the example and says أفعل always takes إفعال. For comparison he gives افتعل–افتعال, with a connected initial alif, such as احتبست احتباسا and انطلقت انطلاقا; استفعل–استفعال, such as استخرجت استخراجا and استصعبت استصعابا; فعل–تفعيل, whose initial ت replaces the extra عين and whose ي corresponds to the alif of إفعال; تفعل–التفعل, retaining letters and damma on عين to avoid confusion with تفعيل; and تفاعل–تفاعل, parallel to تفعل and with damma to avoid a plural-like form. He says speakers of كذابا also say تحملت تحمالا, extending an إفعال-like alif. The fixed فاعل source is مفاعلة, whose م and ة compensate for two alifs, as in جالسته مجالسة and قاعدته مقاعدة, though forms such as قيتالا, مراء and قتالا also occur; فعال is common while مفاعلة is regular."}]}
{"id": "71:18/q06", "question": "Why is إخراجا added after the verb?", "turns_on": "Which feature of the wording is being explained: emphatic verbal noun, bodily identity, or matching verse endings.", "positions": [{"id": "71:18/q06/p1", "position": "The verbal noun emphatically confirms that God will bring people out and that resurrection is certain.", "reasons": "Tabrisi says it emphasizes the act; Razi intensifies the assertion; Baydawi makes the promised return as certain as initial creation; Nasafi and Abu Hayyan stress certainty. {"id": "71:18/q08", "question": "How does this verse fit the surrounding passage and sura?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize different transitions and scales of context; Islahi alone records a choice over who speaks in verses 15–20.", "positions": [{"id": "71:18/q08/p1", "position": "The passage moves from human beginnings to death and future emergence.", "reasons": "Elmalili says the earlier stages give way to humanity's end. {"id": "71:18/q09", "question": "What details of the neighboring wording are noted with this verse?", "turns_on": "These notes concern different nearby expressions and do not record a common dispute.", "positions": [{"id": "71:18/q09/p1", "position": "فجاج denotes broad branching roads, while a فج can be a mountain pass.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives both senses for the neighboring wording."}, {"id": "71:18/q09/p2", "position": "ديار derives from دوران, with an original waw turned to ya and assimilated.", "reasons": "Tabrisi reports al-Zajjaj's explanation that ما بالدار ديار means no one is moving about there."}, {"id": "71:18/q09/p3", "position": "A poet used connected ديار where separated wording was expected, by poetic necessity.", "reasons": "Tabrisi cites the line as an example of unusual connected wording."}, {"id": "71:18/q09/p4", "position": "The object of أسررت is omitted and understood as supplication, warning or the like.", "reasons": "Burhan says a source-like form can coexist with the ellipsis because it need not convey literal emphasis."}, {"id": "71:18/q09/p5", "position": "إسرارا can fit the omitted object because it serves rhyme, or because أسررت becomes intransitive once its object is disregarded.", "reasons": "Burhan compares the second explanation with 'he gives and withholds'; the two explanations are alternatives in the note."}, {"id": "71:18/q09/p6", "position": "A synonym rather than a verb's own source can supply emphasis.", "reasons": "Burhan gives جهارا as a kind of الدعاء, ليا as a kind of distortion, and perhaps بهتانا as a kind of wrongdoing."}, {"id": "71:18/q09/p7", "position": "The second verbal construction can convey ease.", "reasons": "Islahi prefers this sense while allowing other interpretations; the note does not name those alternatives."}]}

{"id": "73:2/q09", "question": "What did early observance of the command look like?", "turns_on": "The transmitted incident or practice being described.", "positions": [{"id": "73:2/q09/p1", "position": "The Prophet and companions maintained long vigils, sometimes all night until their feet or legs swelled.", "reasons": "Qatāda, al-Ḥasan, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, ʿĀʾisha and others report the hardship. {"id": "73:2/q10", "question": "How long did the first night-vigil regime last?", "turns_on": "The differing transmitted interval between the opening command and its easing.", "positions": [{"id": "73:2/q10/p1", "position": "About one year.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿĀʾisha reports place roughly a year between the opening and ending of the sūra; Qatāda sometimes says twelve months.
